_note: AI competencies, groups, definitions, behaviour anchors and the reasons why follow VERBUND's internal concept 'Kompetenzmodell goes AI' (15.10.2026, dimension 'Miteinander | AI nutzen'), translated into English by the student team; use approved by VERBUND (22.11.2026). Everything else is a student-team draft built on the team's interviews and desk research: the three levels, the cases and written tasks of the self-check, the conversation questions, the job examples, the three general competencies (VERBUND's own general competencies were not available to the team), the tasks today and in 2030 per job family, the target profiles that follow from them, the personas and the measures. Course links are examples; entries of VERBUND's catalogue are assumed to exist.

levels.name: Foundation
levels.short: Knows the basics and the rules

levels.name: Practitioner
levels.short: Applies it independently in the own job

levels.name: Advanced
levels.short: Shapes it for others and for the unit

groups.name: Base competencies
groups.note: For everyone: the foundation of any AI use

groups.name: Future competencies
groups.note: For everyone: where AI creates value

groups.name: General competencies
groups.note: For everyone: what the changing job needs beyond AI

competencies.name: Using AI safely
competencies.description: Uses suitable, approved AI tools competently and responsibly in daily work, within the relevant rules.
competencies.definition: Using AI safely means applying AI tools competently, thoughtfully and responsibly in one's own daily work. This includes using suitable and approved AI tools that fit the task, critically checking AI-generated results and taking their limits into account. The relevant rules are followed and data and information are handled responsibly. Responsibility for the use and the resulting work stays with the person.
competencies.question: Which AI tools do you use in your work, and how do you decide what you may enter?
levels: Knows the approved tools and the rules for data and confidentiality.
Applies the rules in daily work without guidance and spots unclear cases.
Advises colleagues on unclear cases and helps to improve the rules.
competencies.why: The foundation of any use: employees must be able to use AI responsibly, safely and in line with legal, ethical and organisational requirements.

weak: Shows little interest in AI applications and their uses.
Uses AI tools not at all or too little in daily work.
Gives too little thought to data protection, confidentiality or legal requirements.
Enters sensitive information into AI systems without thinking.
good: Uses AI applications regularly in daily work.
Uses AI tools sensibly to work more productively.
Observes data protection, security and compliance requirements when using AI.
Knows the strengths and limits of the AI tools used.
Decides consciously when AI should be used and when not.
overdone: Dwells on risks so much that useful applications are prevented.
Avoids productive AI use out of excessive caution.
Uses AI tools excessively or with little value for the own work.

examples.A: Decides which code and data may go into a coding assistant.
examples.B: Knows that contracts and personal data do not belong in a public chatbot.
examples.D: Uses only released tools for plant data and maintenance reports.
examples.M: Makes sure the team knows the rules and where to ask.

cases.title: A quick summary
cases.situation: You have to summarise a long document for a meeting in an hour. It contains names of customers and contract figures. A free AI chatbot on the internet would do it in seconds.

options.text: I do not use the free chatbot for this. I know that such data may only go into approved tools.
I paste the document into the chatbot; the summary is only for internal use anyway.
I use the approved company tool, leave out what it does not need, and check the summary before I pass it on.
I use the approved tool, and because the question comes up often I write down for my team which data may go where.

cases.title: Code in the assistant
cases.situation: You are fixing a bug in a system that handles plant data. The coding assistant would help more if you gave it the whole module, including the configuration file with access data.

options.text: I give it everything; the faster the bug is fixed, the better.
I give it the code it needs, remove access data and anything confidential first, and use only the released assistant.
I am not sure what is allowed, so I ask before I paste anything.
I remove secrets first, and I suggest a rule or an automatic check for the team so that access data cannot end up in prompts.

cases.title: A contract to compare
cases.situation: A colleague asks you to compare two supplier contracts with an AI tool. They contain prices and personal data of contact persons.

options.text: I know that contracts and personal data do not belong in a public chatbot, and I say so.
I use the approved tool, and I prepare a short checklist for the team on what to remove from contracts before using AI.
I upload both contracts to the tool that gives the best comparison.
I use the approved tool, remove the personal data that is not needed, and check the comparison against the contracts.

cases.title: A photo from the plant
cases.situation: On site you find damage you cannot classify. An AI app on your private phone could analyse a photo. The photo would show parts of the plant and its labelling.

options.text: I use only the released tool for plant data, or I send the photo to the responsible engineer the usual way.
I use the app; it is the fastest way to get an answer.
I do not use the private app, because plant data may only go into released tools.
I use the released way, and I report that we need a released tool for such cases, so that nobody uses private apps.

cases.title: A tool the team likes
cases.situation: Two people in your team use a new AI tool they found themselves. It saves them time. It is not on the list of approved tools.

options.text: I point them to the rules and the list of approved tools.
I let them continue; the results are what counts.
I stop the use for company data, have the tool checked the official way, and make sure the whole team knows the rules and where to ask.
I clarify with them which data they entered, stop the use for company data and ask the responsible unit whether the tool can be approved.

tasks.title: A time you decided against AI
tasks.task: Think of a situation at work in which you did not use AI, or used it differently, because of the data or the rules.
lookFor: Decided on the own judgement in an unclear case and found a way that works.
Passed the case on: advised colleagues or suggested a change to the rules.

competencies.name: Checking and owning AI results
competencies.description: Questions AI output critically, judges its quality and plausibility, and stays responsible for how it is used.
competencies.definition: Checking and owning AI results means questioning AI-generated content critically and judging its quality, plausibility and reliability on a sound basis. This requires enough subject, method and AI knowledge to spot errors, bias or gaps and to judge results in their context. Responsibility for using the results stays with the person.
competencies.question: Tell me about a case where an AI result was wrong or incomplete. How did you notice?
levels: Knows that AI output can be wrong and checks facts before using it.
Verifies output systematically with sources, plausibility checks or a second person.
Defines quality checks for the team and trains others in them.
competencies.why: AI produces suggestions, not truth. Judging results critically, placing them in context and taking responsibility for their use becomes a key skill of professional work.

weak: Takes over AI-generated content without checking it.
Does not question sources, assumptions or results enough.
Finds it hard to spot errors, bias or hallucinations.
Does not disclose AI-generated results, or not enough.
Lacks the basic knowledge needed to check AI results properly.
good: Checks AI results critically for plausibility, quality and relevance.
Has a routine and checks for verifying AI results.
Discloses AI-generated results as such where needed.
Takes responsibility for using AI-generated content.
Uses own expertise to place AI results in context.
overdone: Questions AI results to a degree that strongly limits productivity and benefit.
Gets lost in detailed checks without visible value.
Distrusts AI results on principle, whatever their quality.

examples.A: Reviews and tests generated code before it is merged.
examples.B: Checks figures and sources of an AI-drafted report against the original data.
examples.D: Compares an AI fault diagnosis with measurements and own experience.
examples.M: Asks how a result was checked before deciding on it.

cases.title: A mistake after the fact
cases.situation: A colleague finds an error in a text you sent out last week. The passage came from an AI tool.

options.text: I correct it. It was my text, so it is my responsibility, even if AI wrote the passage.
I correct it, inform the recipients, and bring the case into the team so that we agree on how AI passages are checked and marked.
I explain that the error came from the AI tool.
I correct it, inform the recipients, and from now on check such passages against the source before sending.

cases.title: Generated code in review
cases.situation: A colleague’s change contains 300 lines of generated code. All automated tests pass. You are the reviewer.

options.text: I review it like any other code, read the logic, and add tests for the edge cases the generated tests miss.
The tests pass, so I approve.
I review it fully, and I propose review rules for generated code that the team adopts.
I look through it and ask the colleague whether they have checked it themselves.

cases.title: A report draft with figures
cases.situation: The assistant has drafted the monthly report, with comments on the deviations. The figures look reasonable.

options.text: I compare the most important figures with the system before I send it.
I check all figures against the source data and rewrite the comments I cannot confirm.
I send it; the assistant takes the figures from the system anyway.
I check it against the source data, and I have defined for the team which checks a report needs before it goes out.

cases.title: A fault diagnosis
cases.situation: The maintenance tool suggests a defective bearing as the cause of a vibration alarm and recommends replacing it.

options.text: I check the suggestion against measurements and history, and I report back when it was wrong, so that the tool and the team learn from it.
I treat the suggestion as a hint and have a look at the plant before anything is ordered.
I order the replacement; the tool has the data.
I compare the suggestion with the measurements and my experience, and only then decide.

cases.title: A proposal on your desk
cases.situation: Your team gives you a proposal for a decision. You know that large parts were prepared with AI.

options.text: I read it more carefully than usual.
I ask how it was checked, and I have agreed with the team how AI-supported work is checked and marked before it reaches me.
I decide on it as on any other proposal; how it was made does not matter.
I ask how the central statements were checked and decide only when that is clear.

tasks.title: An AI result you used
tasks.task: Take an AI result you used at work in the last weeks. If you have none, produce one now with the approved tool for a task of yours.
prompts: How did you check the result?
What did you change, and what did you pass on?
lookFor: Read the result and checked whether it is plausible.
Describes concrete checks against a source, the figures or the own expertise, and what was corrected.
Describes a routine or checklist that others use, or how the case changed the way the team checks.

competencies.name: Recognising and shaping AI potential
competencies.description: Looks at tasks and processes for where AI creates real value, assesses the potential and develops concrete ideas.
competencies.definition: Recognising and shaping AI potential means looking systematically at tasks, processes and challenges for where AI can create concrete value. This includes identifying and assessing potential and developing concrete ideas and approaches for using AI effectively in one's own work environment.
competencies.question: Where in your work would AI help most? What would it take to try it?
levels: Can name tasks in the own job that AI could support.
Describes a use case with benefit, data needed and risks.
Prioritises use cases for the unit and brings them into the decision process.
competencies.why: Value does not come from technology alone but from using it sensibly. Employees need to see where AI really helps, then assess these ideas and develop them further.

weak: Develops hardly any own ideas or use cases for AI.
Looks at AI options in isolation instead of thinking along processes, roles, data and existing solutions.
Thinks of AI as single functions rather than new or fundamentally changed solutions.
Sees AI mainly as a technical topic, without its effects on ways of working, collaboration or value creation.
good: Recognises and names tasks, processes and challenges where AI can create concrete value.
Thinks in processes and can improve them with AI.
Considers AI actively in improvements, changes and innovation.
Assesses AI potential for cost and benefit, feasibility and relevant conditions.
Develops concrete ideas and approaches from the potential found.
Connects business needs with what AI can do and turns them into sensible scenarios.
Follows new AI developments and transfers relevant options to the own work environment.
overdone: Tries to find an AI solution for every problem, even without visible benefit.
Overestimates what AI can do and underestimates limits, risks or prerequisites.
Pursues AI ideas too quickly, without checking benefit, cost, feasibility and impact.
Overlooks simpler, proven or more economical alternatives.

examples.A: Sees where tests, documentation or monitoring can be supported by AI.
examples.B: Spots recurring reports or enquiries that an assistant could prepare.
examples.D: Suggests where inspection data could point to maintenance needs earlier.
examples.M: Collects ideas from the team and brings the best ones forward.

cases.title: An idea in the team meeting
cases.situation: A colleague suggests using AI for a task in your area. You doubt that it is worth the effort.

options.text: I estimate benefit, effort and feasibility together with the colleague, and also look at simpler alternatives.
I assess it with a fixed set of criteria we use for all AI ideas, so that the decision can be followed.
I leave the assessment to others; I cannot judge AI ideas.
I say what speaks for and against it from my experience.

tasks.title: A task AI could change
tasks.task: Pick one recurring task of your job.
prompts: What is the task, and how much time does it take?
Where would AI help, and what would it need?
What could go wrong, and is there a simpler way?
lookFor: Names a task and the part AI could support.
Describes the whole process, the benefit, the data needed and the risks.
Compares it with other tasks of the unit and says how the idea would be decided and brought forward.

competencies.name: Realising and scaling AI use cases
competencies.description: Turns AI potential into working solutions, alone or with technical experts, and spreads what works.
competencies.definition: Realising and scaling AI use cases means turning AI potential into concrete solutions and integrating them effectively into processes and workflows. This includes combining suitable tools and technologies, implementing solutions oneself or with others, and extending successful applications systematically to further areas.
competencies.question: Have you built or configured an AI solution yourself, for example a prompt template, an agent or an automation?
levels: Uses templates and solutions that others have built.
Builds simple solutions for the own work and shares them.
Develops solutions for several teams and takes care of operation and quality.
competencies.why: The full value of AI comes from consistent use in broader scenarios. What counts is realising use cases with AI, through own technical skill or together with others, making successful solutions visible, passing them on and spreading them in the organisation.

weak: Does not share successful AI applications, prompts or approaches, or too little.
Documents experience, lessons and good practice too little for others to build on.
Thinks of AI mainly within the own area and misses chances to transfer it to other areas.
good: Implements AI use cases independently or together with technical experts.
Chooses suitable AI tools and technologies and combines them for the use case.
Tests and improves AI solutions step by step until they reliably help in daily work.
Makes successful AI solutions reusable and transfers them to further tasks or areas.
Supports others in adopting, adapting and developing successful AI solutions.
overdone: Tries to standardise or spread AI solutions before they are tested enough.
Scales successful applications to other areas too quickly, without their specific needs.
Promotes spreading AI solutions more than their actual benefit and lasting effect.

examples.A: Builds an agent or a pipeline and looks after operation and quality.
examples.B: Sets up a prompt template for a recurring report and shares it.
examples.D: Configures an assistant for standard maintenance documentation.
examples.M: Makes sure a working solution is handed over and reused in other teams.

cases.title: From pilot to daily use
cases.situation: A small AI solution works well for you and one colleague. Other teams are interested.

options.text: I adapt it to their needs with them, document it, and clarify who runs and maintains it.
I have not built or set up an AI solution so far.
I improve it until it works reliably and show the other teams how to use it.
I point them to the person who built it; I only use it.

tasks.title: Something you built or reuse
tasks.task: Think of a prompt, a template or a small AI solution you built, adapted or reuse. If there is none: which one would you build first?
lookFor: Uses templates or solutions others built and can say what for.
Built or adapted something, improved it until it worked, and shared it.
Runs a solution that several teams use, and names documentation, maintenance and quality.

competencies.name: Steering AI use
competencies.description: Gives direction and priorities for AI in the own area and creates the conditions for effective, responsible use.
competencies.definition: Steering AI use means giving orientation and priorities for the use of AI and creating the conditions for effective and responsible use. Managers decide where and for what AI is used, provide suitable resources and make sure that benefit, impact, chances and risks are considered. They set clear conditions and responsibilities and steer the use and development of AI in their area.
competencies.question: How do you decide where your team uses AI, and how do you follow what comes out of it?
levels: Knows where the team already uses AI.
Sets goals and priorities for AI use and reviews results regularly.
Aligns AI use with the unit's strategy and with data, process and project needs.
competencies.why: The value of AI comes from using it on purpose. Managers have to decide where AI creates real value, which risks to consider and which priorities to set.

weak: Hardly takes up AI topics in the own area and sets no visible priorities.
Sees relevant uses and potential of AI for the own area only partly.
Hardly considers the effects, chances and risks of AI in decisions and plans.
Gives little orientation on where, for what and under which conditions AI should be used.
Creates hardly any conditions for effective AI use.
Encourages neither learning nor experimenting in the team.
good: Develops a target picture for AI use in the own area.
Builds the AI knowledge needed, alone or in the team, to judge and drive developments.
Makes room for learning, trying out and sharing experience.
Builds AI competencies in the team.
Gives orientation on chances, risks and expectations.
Supports employees in integrating AI sensibly into their work.
Works out sensible cost-benefit considerations for AI with the team.
Develops a positive and realistic picture of how people and AI will work together.
overdone: Goes for technically demanding AI solutions even where simpler ones would fit better.
Pushes new AI technologies without weighing benefit, maturity and feasibility.
Uses AI solutions without considering data quality, infrastructure, security or integration.
Focuses on technical possibilities and neglects business, organisational or economic needs.

examples.M: Sets two or three AI goals for the team and reviews them every quarter.

cases.title: After six months
cases.situation: Your team has had AI licences for half a year. Usage differs a lot between people.

options.text: I look at where it helps, set two or three goals for the team and review them regularly.
I have not looked at how the licences are used.
I know who uses AI for what.
I adjust goals, time and support from the results, and bring what we learned into the unit’s planning.

tasks.title: Your priorities for AI
tasks.task: Think of the goals or priorities you set for AI in your area this year.
prompts: How do you follow what comes out of them?
lookFor: Knows where the team uses AI.
Names goals or priorities and a regular review.
Links them to the unit’s strategy and to data, security and budget.

competencies.name: Guiding the AI change
competencies.description: Shapes how AI changes work in the team: gives orientation, takes up concerns and makes room to learn.
competencies.definition: Guiding the AI change means shaping the changes AI brings to work and collaboration actively and deliberately. Managers give orientation, make goals and effects understandable and involve employees in the change. They take up uncertainty and resistance, make room for learning and experimenting and support their teams in building new skills. They encourage sharing experience and make sure new ways of working take root step by step.
competencies.question: What do you do so that all team members, also the hesitant ones, get started with AI?
levels: Uses AI visibly in the own work and talks about it.
Plans learning time, addresses concerns and uses role models in the team.
Builds a learning culture across teams and develops other managers.
competencies.why: AI is not only a technology rollout but a deep change of work, roles and collaboration. Managers have to give orientation, build acceptance and guide the change actively.

weak: Avoids talking about the effects of AI on the team, tasks or collaboration.
Gives little orientation on chances, risks and expectations around AI.
Leaves uncertainty, concerns or resistance unaddressed.
Does too little for learning, sharing and experimenting with AI.
Gives employees too little support with new requirements and ways of working.
Recognises support and development needs around AI too late.
good: Gives orientation in phases of AI-driven change.
Makes the reasons, goals and effects of AI initiatives understandable.
Addresses chances, risks and uncertainties of the AI transformation openly.
Takes concerns and resistance seriously and deals with them constructively.
Encourages a positive, learning-oriented attitude to change.
Supports teams in trying out and developing new ways of working.
Supports teams in integrating AI successfully into their daily work.
Builds acceptance, participation and co-design rather than mere instruction.
Spots support needs early and sets targeted measures to guide the change.
overdone: Pushes AI changes too fast or too hard, without regard for the team's capacity.
Focuses so much on AI that other team and leadership tasks suffer.
Demands readiness for change without giving enough time to learn and adapt.
Overestimates the team's readiness or ability to take on new ways of working at once.
Is so enthusiastic about AI that risks, limits or justified concerns get too little attention.

examples.M: Blocks learning time and shows the own use of AI in team meetings.

cases.title: No time to learn
cases.situation: Your team says there is no time to try AI tools next to the daily work.

options.text: I show how I use AI myself and encourage them to try.
I fix learning time in the calendar, set up exchange across teams and help other managers to do the same.
I plan fixed learning time, and we look together at what can be dropped for it.
I tell them to use the tools when there is time.

tasks.title: Someone who hesitated
tasks.task: Think of a team member who was unsure or hesitant about AI.
lookFor: Took the concern seriously, gave time to learn and a role model.
Turned it into something for the whole team or for other managers.

competencies.name: Working with data
competencies.description: Reads, questions and maintains the data the own work and the AI tools rely on.
competencies.question: Which data does your work rely on, and how do you know it is good enough?
levels: Knows which data the own tasks use and reports obvious errors.
Checks data quality before using it and feeds corrections back to the source.
Sets data standards for the team and improves how data is collected and shared.
competencies.why: AI results are only as good as the data behind them. In all focus families the work moves from producing data and reports to judging and maintaining them.

examples.A: Looks after data quality and access in pipelines and interfaces.
examples.B: Knows where the figures of a report come from and spots when they cannot be right.
examples.D: Records inspection and maintenance data so that it can be used later.
examples.M: Asks which data a proposal rests on and how good it is.

cases.title: Figures that do not match
cases.situation: For your task you take data from a system. Two figures do not match what you know from practice.

options.text: I use the data as it is; it comes from the system.
I notice it and report it to someone who is responsible.
I clarify the cause, have it corrected at the source, and suggest a check so that it is noticed earlier next time.
I check where the figures come from before I use them, and have the error corrected at the source.

competencies.name: Adapting and learning
competencies.description: Takes up new tools and ways of working and builds the skills they need.
competencies.question: What was the last tool or way of working you had to learn? How did you go about it?
levels: Takes up new tools and ways of working when they are introduced.
Tries new tools on the own tasks early and builds the missing skills on purpose.
Helps others through changes and shapes how the team learns.
competencies.why: Tools and tasks will change several times until 2030. Studies of the energy sector and the team's interviews name adaptability and continuous learning as key competencies.

examples.A: Keeps up with new models and tools and tries them on real work.
examples.B: Moves from entering data to handling exceptions and learns the tools for it.
examples.D: Works with digital assistants on site and operates several systems side by side.
examples.M: Learns visibly and plans time for the team to do the same.

cases.title: A new tool replaces a familiar one
cases.situation: A tool you know well is replaced. The new one works differently and includes AI functions.

options.text: I try it on my real tasks early and look for the training I need.
I take part in the training and use it once it is introduced.
I keep to the old way as long as possible.
I try it early, pass on what I learn and help colleagues who struggle with the change.

competencies.name: Thinking in processes and solving problems
competencies.description: Understands the process around the own task and solves new problems in a structured way.
competencies.question: Tell me about a problem that was not covered by any instruction. How did you solve it?
levels: Knows the own step in the process and solves routine problems.
Understands the process from end to end and solves new problems in a structured way.
Redesigns processes across teams and leads others through complex problems.
competencies.why: Routine steps are automated; what stays with people are the exceptions and the improvement of the process. Problem-solving gains strongly in technical jobs, process skills in management.

examples.A: Designs integrations with the whole process in mind, across IT and plant systems.
examples.B: Handles the cases the automation cannot and improves the process behind them.
examples.D: Narrows down faults that no tool has seen before.
examples.M: Redesigns how work is shared between people and AI in the own area.

cases.title: A problem nobody has had before
cases.situation: A step in your work fails in a way that is not described anywhere. Others are waiting for your result.

options.text: I solve what I can in my own step and pass the rest on.
I find the cause across the whole process with the others involved, and change the process so that it does not happen again.
I narrow down the cause step by step, look at the steps before and after mine, and solve it.
I wait until someone tells me what to do.

families.name: Software, IT & Data
families.summary: Builds and runs the digital systems. Highest AI exposure and the role of multiplier.
families.example: e.g. coding assistants, automated testing, data pipelines with AI checks

tasks.today: Developers write most code by hand and review each other’s changes.
tasks.future: AI writes a large share of the code. The developer specifies, reviews and tests it and answers for what is merged.

tasks.today: Tests and documentation are written by hand, often late.
tasks.future: Generated by AI and checked by the team. The effort moves to the test strategy and the edge cases.

tasks.today: Interfaces and data pipelines are built per project; data quality is checked case by case.
tasks.future: Integration, data access and data quality decide whether an AI use case works, across IT and plant systems.

tasks.today: First pilots with assistants and single models.
tasks.future: Agents and AI services are built, monitored and scaled for several units, with security and operation in mind.

tasks.today: IT implements what the units ask for.
tasks.future: IT is the multiplier: it finds use cases with the units, judges what is feasible and keeps up with new tools.

personas.name: Beginner
personas.story: Uses the coding assistant now and then for small snippets. Knows the rules, but is unsure which data may go into a prompt.

personas.name: Advanced
personas.story: Works with AI every day, reviews generated code carefully and has built templates the team uses.

personas.name: Expert
personas.story: Builds agents and pipelines for several teams, sets the checks others use and is asked about unclear cases.

families.basis: Interviews and desk research of the student team, as summarised for the jour fixe of 24.11.2026; wording and levels are a draft.

families.name: Commercial & Corporate Office
families.summary: Finance, procurement, HR, legal and administration. Text- and data-heavy work.
families.example: e.g. report drafts, contract summaries, analysis of supplier data

tasks.today: Figures are collected from several systems; reports are built by hand in spreadsheets.
tasks.future: Standard reports and bookings are produced automatically. People check the figures, explain deviations and answer for the result.

tasks.today: Research, minutes, mails and first drafts are written by hand.
tasks.future: An assistant prepares research, texts and analyses. The person briefs it, checks the output and decides what goes out.

tasks.today: Documents are read, entered and matched by hand.
tasks.future: Entry and matching run automatically. Staff handle the exceptions and improve the process.

tasks.today: Contracts, supplier data and personal data are handled under the existing confidentiality rules.
tasks.future: The same rules decide what may go into which AI tool. Staff judge unclear cases themselves.

tasks.today: Improvements come up from case to case.
tasks.future: Staff name where an assistant helps, use the templates others built and take up new tools quickly.

personas.name: Beginner
personas.story: Has tried the chatbot a few times. Is unsure what may be entered and uses results as they come.

personas.name: Advanced
personas.story: Uses the assistant every week for drafts and analyses and checks the figures against the source.

personas.name: Expert
personas.story: Has built prompt templates the team uses. Colleagues ask about unclear cases.

families.basis: Interviews and desk research of the student team, as summarised for the jour fixe of 24.11.2026; wording and levels are a draft.

families.name: Engineering & Technicians
families.summary: Plans, builds and maintains the plants. AI supports, physical work stays.
families.example: e.g. AI-supported CAD, simulation, maintenance and process analysis

tasks.today: Inspections follow fixed intervals; findings are judged from experience.
tasks.future: AI points to maintenance needs from inspection and sensor data. Technicians check the hint against measurements and experience before they act.

tasks.today: Maintenance reports and plant documentation are written by hand after the job.
tasks.future: An assistant drafts the documentation. The technician corrects it and feeds good data back.

tasks.today: Designs and simulations are set up by hand.
tasks.future: AI proposes variants in CAD and simulation. Engineers check whether they are plausible and stay responsible for the design.

tasks.today: Faults are narrowed down step by step with measurements and manuals.
tasks.future: AI suggests likely causes. New and complex faults stay with people.

tasks.today: Manual work on site: assembly, switching, repairs.
tasks.future: Changes least. Digital assistants give instructions and record the work; several systems are operated side by side.

personas.name: Beginner
personas.story: Works mainly on site and has not used AI tools at work so far.

personas.name: Advanced
personas.story: Uses the released tools for documentation and analysis and compares AI hints with measurements.

personas.name: Expert

tasks.today: Goals follow the unit’s plan; AI is one topic among many.
tasks.future: Managers decide where AI is used in their area, with which priority and under which rules.

tasks.task: Deciding on the basis of reports
tasks.today: Decisions rest on reports the team prepares.
tasks.future: Much of the basis is prepared with AI. Managers ask how it was checked and stay accountable.

tasks.today: Change is led project by project.
tasks.future: AI changes tasks and roles continuously. Managers give orientation, plan learning time and take up concerns.

tasks.today: Development is agreed in the yearly appraisal talk.
tasks.future: The competency conversation is part of it: managers know the AI levels in their team and agree on measures.

tasks.task: Using AI in the own work
tasks.today: Own use differs strongly between managers.
tasks.future: Leaders go first: they use AI visibly themselves and reuse what their teams built.

personas.name: Beginner

personas.name: Advanced

personas.name: Expert
personas.story: Has a target picture for AI and reviews the results. Other managers copy the approach.

measures.title: Starter training on approved tools and data rules
measures.description: Before a licence is handed out, so that licences do not stay unused. From “What is AI?” to the rules for data and confidentiality, repeated every year.

courses.title: AI Academy: basics and the AI Act

measures.title: Workshop on checking AI output
measures.description: Review of AI output as part of quality assurance, on real tasks from the team, with a four-eyes check for critical results.

measures.title: Use-case workshop in the team
measures.description: Small groups work on use cases from their own job and assess benefit, effort and feasibility.

measures.title: Hands-on sessions on prompting, templates and agents
measures.description: Learning by doing on a real use case, with a mentor. Follows the starter training: first prompting, then building agents.

measures.title: Leadership programme on AI
measures.description: Leaders go first: steering AI use, leading the change, peer exchange between managers.

measures.title: Programme for changing roles
measures.description: For employees whose tasks change strongly, for example from data entry to exception handling, or towards data and automation work. Internal conversion before hiring.

measures.title: Hire for scarce specialist skills
measures.description: Upskilling first, hiring for specialists: where the gap to the advanced level cannot be closed in time by training. With an entry route for juniors.

measures.title: Target profile in job ads and selection
measures.description: The profile of the job family becomes part of job ads and interviews.

measures.title: AI champions, AI café and office hours
measures.description: Role models in the units who help colleagues, collect use cases and show what they built.

measures.title: Planned time to try
measures.description: Agreed hours per month in the team calendar. The yearly education time can be used for it.

measures.title: Data basics for the own job
measures.description: Where the data of the own tasks comes from, how to judge its quality and how to feed corrections back.

courses.title: Courses on data and AI, in German

measures.title: Learning routine and problem-solving
measures.description: Short formats on learning new tools on the job and on structured problem-solving, with cases from the unit.

Managers and employees agree on levels.
HR reads the aggregated gaps; Learning & Development adjusts the offer.
What did the measures change? Input for the next review.

rules: The check serves development. It is not used for pay, appraisal or staffing decisions.
Levels are agreed by two people in a conversation. No AI rates anyone.
The self-check belongs to the employee. The manager sees it only if the employee shares it.
A manager sees the own team. HR sees totals only, never single persons.
Groups with fewer than five rated employees are not shown.
Employees can see everything stored about them and ask for corrections.
Entries are replaced by next year's conversation.
Purpose, access and retention are fixed in a works agreement (Betriebsvereinbarung) before any real use.
